sections.title: Theaters, audience areas, and performance spaces
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 520 takes theaters, audience areas of movie and television studios, and performance areas out of Article 518 and gives them their own rules, built around stage and house lighting, switchboards, and portable stage equipment. Wiring methods echo the assembly rules, with added provisions for the portable and temporary-looking equipment that is actually permanent in a theater. Sharma would meet this on a school auditorium or church stage package, not on ordinary tenant work.

For scope-spotting: fixed stage switchboards, portable switchboards used on stage, and the flexible cables and connectors feeding portable stage equipment are the article's center of gravity, and its wiring-method rules are stricter than ordinary commercial work because audiences sit in the dark in front of energized equipment. Any Sharma bid touching a stage should carry the article as a named scope with engineered drawings — it is never a 'few extra dimmers' add-on.
sections.on_the_job: Treat any stage, dimming, or performance lighting scope as engineered work and price only detailed plans. Portable stage cable and connectors follow this article, not jobsite temporary rules.

sections.title: Control systems for permanent amusement attractions
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 522 covers the control systems of permanent amusement attractions — the rides and attractions built to stay, as opposed to the traveling shows in Article 525. It covers control circuit power sources and control circuit conductors, not the ride's power circuits: the motor feeder that delivers the horsepower belongs to the general chapters; the wiring that tells the motor what to do belongs here. Where 522 and another article differ, 522 applies (522.3).
• Control voltage is capped at 150 volts ac to ground or 300 volts dc to ground (522.5).
• Power-limited control circuits are supplied from a source rated not more than 30 volts and 1,000 volt-amperes; a source other than a transformer gets overcurrent protection at not more than 167 percent of its volt-ampere rating divided by its rated voltage (522.10(A)).
• Non-power-limited control circuits may run up to 300 volts, with source overcurrent protection at not more than 125 percent on the same basis (522.10(B)).
• Control circuit conductors are copper — aluminum conductors are not permitted (522.20).
• Where wet contact is likely, ungrounded 2-wire control circuits are limited to 30 volts dc (522.28).
• Only qualified persons service the attraction (522.7).
It is a narrow article most electricians meet only on attraction work.
sections.on_the_job: A permanent carousel and coaster package lands in a Central Florida attraction expansion. If an attraction appears in a scope, stop at the intro level and get the manufacturer's and engineer's control package. Do not improvise ride controls from general-purpose relays. When the package arrives, the Sharma scope reads from it: control panels fed from a 24-volt power-limited source of 1,000 VA or less sit inside 522.10(A); any control run the package shows at 120 volts is non-power-limited work, capped at 300 volts; and every control conductor is copper — the value-engineering suggestion to save money with aluminum control wire is a violation here (522.20).
sections.why_it_exists: Ride controls are the safety system. They carry the start, stop and interlock signals that keep a moving machine from hurting the people on it. Capping control voltage and giving control circuits their own power-source rules keeps a fault in a pushbutton circuit from becoming a fault at line voltage, and keeps the signals honest and alive when the power side is in trouble.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is wiring ride controls like ordinary remote-control circuits out of the general chapters and stopping there. Article 522 has its own power-source rules: power-limited means a source of not more than 30 volts and 1,000 VA (522.10(A)), overall control voltage is capped at 150 volts ac or 300 volts dc to ground (522.5), and where 522 differs from the other articles, 522 wins (522.3).

sections.title: Carnivals, circuses, fairs, and similar events
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 525 covers temporary event power for carnivals, circuses, fairs, and similar events — rides, games, food stands, and show wiring that is installed and removed for each event. It works alongside Article 590 but adds event-specific rules that 590 does not contain.
• Disconnects at the operator. Each ride and concession gets a fused disconnect switch or circuit breaker within sight of, and within 6 ft of, the operator's station (525.21).
• GFCI where the public is. All 15 A and 20 A, 125 V nonlocking receptacles used for assembly and disassembly, or accessible to the public, get GFCI protection — and so does public-accessible equipment on 15 A or 20 A, 120 V circuits (525.23). Locking-type receptacles are exempt, and GFCI protection is not permitted on egress lighting circuits.
• Overhead clearance. Rides and attractions stay at least 15 ft clear of overhead conductors (525.5).
• Cords do the work. Portable cords are of a type identified for extra-hard usage, 12 AWG or larger, of the grounding type, and protected where they cross walkways or traffic (525.20).
• Bonding at every setup. Metal frames of rides, concessions, and equipment fed from the same source are bonded together (525.30), and the continuity of the equipment grounding conductor is verified each time portable equipment is connected (525.32).
sections.on_the_job: Event power is not ordinary temp power — check this article as well as 590 before quoting a fair or festival job. On a Sharma quote for a fair weekend in Osceola County, the layout shows a temp service, distribution boxes on stands 6 in. off the ground, and a disconnect within 6 ft of each ride operator's station. The takeoff counts GFCI protection for every public-side 20 A, 125 V receptacle, extra-hard-usage cord for the runs, and a line item for the grounding continuity check at setup. Operator disconnects and ride grounding are priced items, not afterthoughts.

The rules assume the installation will be handled, walked on, and rained on: the operator can kill a ride from his own station, the public side is GFCI-protected, and the ground path is proven at every setup instead of assumed from the last one.

sections.title: Carnivals and fairs — GFCI protection for personnel (525.23)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 525.23 requires ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel on:
• The 15 A and 20 A, 125-volt, single-phase receptacles readily accessible to the general public.
• Equipment readily accessible to the general public that is supplied from a 15 A or 20 A, 120-volt branch circuit (525.23(A)).
That is the rule at carnivals, circuses, fairs, and similar events. Portable distribution at an event is temporary power with the public standing on the ground: the GFCI rule is the point of the article for a service electrician, and it applies to the event hookup even when the same box would be ordinary temporary power on a construction site under Article 590.
• GFCI is not required on receptacles that are not accessible from grade level and serve only quick-disconnect connections for amusement rides (525.23(B)).
• Egress lighting may not be GFCI protected (525.23(C)) — a nuisance trip must not be able to darken the way out.
sections.on_the_job: Fairground and festival hookups: test every GFCI at setup, and again after any generator refuel-and-restart cycle. A nuisance trip on a midway is an annoyance; a missing GFCI is a liability. On a county-fair hookup, walk the row before the gates open: every public receptacle on the distro boxes is 15 A or 20 A, 125-volt, so every one gets GFCI protection for personnel; the ride operator's quick-disconnect receptacles mounted up on the ride frame, out of reach from grade, are the 525.23(B) case and are left unprotected by design; the egress lighting circuit is landed on a plain breaker, never a GFCI (525.23(C)).
sections.figure_idea: Event distro box with GFCI test arrows and the 15/20 A, 125 V receptacle row highlighted.
sections.florida_note: Florida's fair and festival season runs through the wet months — assume the ground is wet for every outdoor event hookup.
sections.why_it_exists: Midway power runs across wet grass and metal ride frames, with kids in sandals and food-truck staff plugging in all day. A fault that would only trip a breaker on a jobsite can put current through a person standing on grade. GFCI protection for personnel is the layer that trips in milliseconds, before the shock becomes a fatality — and the egress rule keeps that same fast trip from blacking out the exit path in a panic.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is protecting everything. An exam answer that puts the egress lighting on a GFCI "for extra safety" is wrong — 525.23(C) prohibits GFCI protection on egress lighting, because a trip during an evacuation leaves the crowd in the dark. The mirror-image trap is skipping GFCI on the public receptacles because the distro box is "only temporary power" — Article 525, not 590, governs the event hookup, and 525.23(A) requires the protection.

sections.title: Motion picture and television studios
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 530 covers studios and similar locations where motion picture or television production happens — sound stages and the areas where film or tape is made, handled and stored — where cameras record but no audience sits (530.1). Audience areas belong to Article 520 instead.
• Permanent wiring is in metal raceways, in nonmetallic raceways encased in at least 2 in of concrete, or in Type MI, Type MC or Type AC cable with an insulated equipment grounding conductor (530.11).
• Portable wiring for set lighting and effects is portable cable and flexible cord; wiring that is subject to physical damage is extra-hard usage cord (530.12).
• Permanently installed stage set lighting feeders are not summed at 100 percent — they take the demand factors of Table 530.7.
• Stage lighting and effects are run from location boards: portable boards with contactors and overcurrent protection, built for remote control of stage lighting.
It exists because studio lighting loads and portable equipment do not behave like ordinary commercial installations. Florida production work is the only likely Sharma encounter.
sections.on_the_job: A production company converts a Winter Park warehouse into a small sound stage and asks Sharma for the stage power. Studio scope is specialty scope — work from the production electrical package. Nothing in this article authorizes studio feeder practices on ordinary jobs. The package shows 180,000 VA of permanently installed stage set lighting: Table 530.7 sizes the feeder at 50,000 × 100% + 50,000 × 75% + 80,000 × 60% = 135,500 VA of demand, not 180,000 VA. Permanent runs go in metal raceway; the set lighting itself is portable cable worked from the location boards.

sections.why_it_exists: A stage is a temporary factory rebuilt for every scene: heavy lighting loads on portable cable, struck and re-rigged daily by crews working fast, often in the dark. The raceway rules protect the permanent skeleton of the building, the cord rules assume portable gear gets dragged, stepped on and driven over, and the demand table recognizes that no production burns every lamp at full at the same moment.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing a studio stage feeder at 100 percent of the connected lighting load. Permanently installed stage set lighting feeders use Table 530.7: the first 50,000 VA at 100 percent, the next 50,000 VA at 75 percent, the next 100,000 VA at 60 percent, and everything over 200,000 VA at 50 percent. The second trap is keeping an audience in the room and staying in 530 — audience areas are Article 520.

sections.title: Motion picture projection rooms
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 540 is a short article covering motion picture projection rooms, projectors and associated equipment, professional and nonprofessional, using incandescent, carbon arc, xenon or other light sources that develop hazardous gases, dust or radiation (540.1).
• Every professional-type projector — 35 mm and 70 mm film machines and the arc and xenon types — sits in a projection room of permanent construction, and every projection, spotlight and viewing port is completely closed with glass or other approved material (540.10).
• A projection room is not a hazardous (classified) location under Article 500 — its rules are fire and equipment rules, not classified-wiring rules (540.10).
• Motor-generator sets, transformers, rectifiers and rheostats are located or guarded so arcs and sparks cannot reach film; with nitrate film, they go in a separate room (540.11).
• Each projector, floodlight and spotlight gets clear working space at least 30 in wide on each side and the rear (540.12).
• Conductors for professional arc and xenon projectors are not smaller than 8 AWG, with ampacity not less than the projector rating (540.13).
• Projectors, lamp enclosures, rectifiers, transformers and rheostats must be listed (540.20).
• A nonprofessional projector using cellulose acetate safety film may operate without a projection room (540.31).
Digital projection has shrunk its footprint, but the article remains in the 2020 book wherever a projection room still exists. Ventilation and equipment placement are its main subjects.
sections.on_the_job: On a theater renovation in Seminole County, confirm whether a projection room is in scope before assuming 518 or 520 covers the whole job. If the room were digital-only, with no professional-type projector, the room mandate falls away and the assembly and theater articles carry the job.
sections.why_it_exists: The article was written for nitrate film, which burns fiercely and carries its own oxygen, in a small room around carbon-arc lamps throwing sparks and heat. The room contains the fire, the closed ports keep flame and smoke out of the auditorium, and the guarding rules keep arcing equipment away from the film. Xenon lamps kept the heat and pressure hazards after nitrate left, so the room rules stayed.

sections.title: Manufactured buildings and relocatable structures
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 545 covers buildings built in a factory in sections or panels and assembled on site, plus relocatable structures such as portable classrooms and jobsite offices. The electrical questions are how the factory-built sections connect together, how the completed building connects to its service, and which parts are inspected at the factory versus on site. Florida's portable classroom and modular office market makes this a live article for Sharma even though this first pass stays at intro level.

Site-side, the work concentrates at two joints: the interconnection between factory-built sections, made with the manufacturer's listed connection system and instructions, and the feeder or service connection to the completed building, which follows the ordinary service and feeder rules once the building is set. Which joint belongs to the factory's inspection and which to the local AHJ is decided by the state modular program paperwork — get it before rough-in, because an unlisted field splice between sections is the finding this article exists to prevent.
sections.on_the_job: On a modular or portable classroom job, get the manufacturer's connection details and the state modular insignia paperwork before pricing the site connection. This page is verified at article level only — no subsection numbers are given on this pass, on purpose.

sections.title: Agricultural buildings
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 547 covers agricultural buildings and areas with excessive dust, dust mixed with water, or a corrosive atmosphere — livestock confinement, dairies, and poultry houses are the Florida cases. It modifies the normal chapters, not replaces them.
• Animals are far more sensitive to small voltages than people — a cow on wet concrete feels differences a person would never notice — so this article fights stray voltage as hard as corrosion.
• Equipotential planes (547.10): where livestock are confined on concrete, a bonded wire mesh plane goes in the floor so the animal's feet and the metal it touches stay at the same voltage. It bonds to the building grounding system with solid copper, 8 AWG or larger, on listed pressure connectors or clamps. The pour is the deadline — the plane cannot be added after.
• Distribution point (547.9): livestock buildings on the same premises are fed from a distribution point in a four-wire grounded arrangement, which keeps neutral current from returning through the earth and the buildings' grounding. More than one point is permitted, and the underground feeders and branch circuits leaving it get overcurrent protection.
• Wiring methods (547.5) must survive damp, wet, and corrosive conditions, with an insulated equipment grounding conductor where the ground runs underground outside a listed cable assembly. GFCI protection covers 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles at equipotential planes, outdoors, in damp or wet locations, and in dirt confinement areas (547.5(G)).
sections.on_the_job: Horse barn and wash rack outside Ocala: the bid asks on day one whether horses will be confined on the concrete aisle. They will, so the takeoff prices the bonded mesh plane and its 8 AWG solid copper bond before the slab pour, one distribution point feeding barn and wash rack in a four-wire run, and GFCI protection on the 125-volt receptacles at the plane and outdoors. Corrosion-resistant methods are priced from the start, not discovered at inspection.

sections.why_it_exists: Two killers share this article. Corrosion eats ordinary boxes, cables, and ground paths until equipment metal sits live in a wet barn. And stray voltage — a volt or two between a waterer and the floor — stresses livestock, cuts production, and is nearly impossible to chase later. The plane, the distribution arrangement, and corrosion-proof methods are one system aimed at both.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: giving every barn its own service drop and its own neutral-to-ground bond because it looks simpler. That is the classic stray-voltage layout — neutral current splits between wire, earth, and grounding systems. 547.9 feeds livestock buildings from a distribution point in a four-wire grounded arrangement instead. Second trap: treating the plane as optional on a concrete confinement floor. Where 547.10 applies, the plane and its 8 AWG solid copper bond are the installation, installed before the pour.

sections.title: Wiring methods in agricultural buildings
sections.plain_explanation:
Agricultural buildings in 547.1(A) and (B) — excessive dust, dust mixed with water, or a corrosive atmosphere — get their own wiring methods, because ordinary methods fill with dust, rot, or corrode through in that air.
• Wiring systems (547.5(A)): Type UF, Type NMC, copper SE cable, jacketed Type MC cable, rigid nonmetallic conduit, liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit, or other cables or raceways suitable for the location, with approved termination fittings. Article 502 methods are permitted in the excessive-dust areas of 547.1(A).
• Boxes, conduit bodies, and fittings (547.5(B)): listed to be dusttight and watertight where the dust, moisture, or corrosive conditions demand it.
• Underground grounding (547.5(F)): an equipment grounding conductor that runs underground has to be insulated — the exception is a grounding conductor that is part of a listed cable assembly.
• GFCI (547.5(G)): 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles need GFCI protection for personnel in four places: areas with an equipotential plane, outdoors, in damp or wet locations, and in dirt confinement areas. Receptacles above that voltage and size are outside the list. One exception: a receptacle outlet for a dedicated load does not need the protection where a GFCI-protected receptacle is located within 3 ft of it.
sections.on_the_job: Polk County dairy, 60 stalls: the parlor is washed down daily, so branch runs are rigid nonmetallic conduit with watertight boxes — nothing metal for the ammonia air to eat. The run out to the milk room goes underground in PVC, and the equipment grounding conductor in that run is insulated, not bare. Every 125-volt, 15- and 20-ampere receptacle in the parlor, at the outdoor wash pad, and along the dirt confinement pens is GFCI protected. The 240-volt receptacle for the pressure washer is outside the 547.5(G) list and is not. The brooder receptacle runs as a dedicated load with a GFCI receptacle within 3 ft, so the exception covers it.
sections.sharma_note: Where GFCI is required here it is personnel protection; a GFCI breaker method can serve where the plans allow it. S-07's device pattern was written for houses — on a barn, follow the plans and this section, not the house pattern by default.
sections.why_it_exists: Manure gases, washdown water, and feed dust attack wiring from the day it is installed. A corroded raceway loses its grounding path, a dust-filled box overheats, and a wet concrete floor turns a small fault into stray voltage that livestock feel long before a person would. These methods keep enclosures sealed and the grounding path alive in that atmosphere.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “every receptacle in the barn needs GFCI.” 547.5(G) covers only 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles, and only in the four listed areas. A 240-volt receptacle for the pressure washer is outside the list — and so is a receptacle in a dry office corner of the same building.

sections.title: Supply from a distribution point — livestock buildings
sections.plain_explanation:
On a farm with several livestock buildings, the buildings do not each get their own service. They are supplied from a distribution point — the supply point, often the center yard pole or meter pole, from which feeders, service drops or laterals run to the agricultural buildings and the farm dwelling under one management. The rules that make the layout work:
• The supply from the distribution point is a four-wire grounded arrangement: ungrounded conductors, an insulated grounded (neutral) conductor, and a separate equipment grounding conductor
• More than one distribution point is expressly permitted on the same premises
• A site-isolating device at the distribution point disconnects the premises from the utility; it is not the service disconnect for the individual buildings
• The neutral is bonded to the grounding system at the distribution point — and nowhere else downstream
• Each building still gets its own grounding electrode system and disconnecting means under 250.32
• Overcurrent protection is required for the underground branch circuits and feeders leaving the distribution point
sections.on_the_job: On a multi-building farm service, draw the distribution point on the site sketch and price the four-wire runs and underground protection as shown. Do not serve each barn with its own improvised service drop and neutral bond. On a Hardee County cattle operation with a dairy barn, a calf barn and the farmhouse on one meter pole, that means three four-wire feeders from the pole, a grounding electrode at the pole and at each building, and neutral and ground bars kept separate in every barn panel — one bond, at the pole, serves the whole farm.
sections.why_it_exists: On an old three-wire farm system, the neutral and the equipment ground share one path, so normal neutral current divides between the wire, the earth, and every bonded water line and stanchion on the place. That shared current is the main on-farm source of stray voltage — the small voltage between two things a cow touches at the same time. The four-wire layout gives neutral current its own insulated road home and keeps it off the earth and the grounding system, so building metal stays at earth potential.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is one service per barn, each with its own neutral-to-ground bond. Every extra bond puts neutral current back on the earth and the grounding system — exactly what 547.9 exists to stop. The second trap is 'only one distribution point is ever allowed on a farm.' The section expressly permits more than one distribution point on the same premises.
inspection_fails: Neutral bonded again in a barn panel fed from the distribution point.
Three-wire feeder — no separate equipment grounding conductor — run to a livestock building.
Underground feeder leaving the distribution point with no overcurrent protection.
Building fed from the distribution point with no grounding electrode system at the building (250.32).
No site-isolating device at the distribution point, or the pole switch treated as each building's service disconnect.

sections.title: Equipotential planes in livestock confinement areas
sections.plain_explanation:
An equipotential plane is a grid of wire mesh or other conductive elements embedded in, or placed under, the concrete floor of a livestock confinement area, bonded together and connected to the building's electrical grounding system. It is required where all of these are true:
• The area confines livestock (the term does not include poultry)
• The floor is concrete — an indoor confinement floor, or an outdoor concrete slab
• Metal equipment that may become energized — waterers, stanchions, feeders, gates — is within the animals' reach
Outdoors, the plane must cover the ground where the animal stands while it touches that equipment. The bonding conductor is solid copper, insulated, covered or bare, not smaller than 8 AWG. Connections to the mesh or conductive elements are made with pressure connectors or clamps of brass, copper, copper alloy, or an equally substantial approved means. Slatted floors supported by a structure that is part of the plane do not need separate bonding.
sections.on_the_job: Coordinate the plane with the concrete crew before the pour — retrofitting a bonded plane after slab placement is not a real option. Keep the 8 AWG solid copper bond and its connections inspectable until they are approved. On a Polk County dairy addition the sequence is: mesh tied, the 8 AWG solid copper bond clamped to the mesh with listed pressure connectors and run to the barn panel's grounding terminal, and a photo of every connection before the pour is scheduled. Remember the companion rule in 547.5(G): 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles in the plane area need GFCI protection.
sections.why_it_exists: A cow standing on wet concrete is in near-perfect contact with the earth, and livestock feel voltages a person in boots never notices. If a fault or neutral current raises a metal waterer even a few volts above the floor under the animal's feet, current passes through the animal every time it drinks — the classic tingle voltage that cuts feed intake and milk production and can kill. The plane removes the difference: floor, waterer and stanchions are held at one voltage, so nothing drives current through the animal.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the plane like a ground rod: drive a separate rod at the pen and call it done. A rod by itself equalizes nothing — the rule is a bonded plane tied to the building grounding system, with a solid copper bonding conductor of at least 8 AWG. The second wrong answer is stranded conductor or a hose clamp on the mesh: the conductor must be solid, and the connections must be pressure connectors or clamps.

Concrete poured before the plane connections were inspected, leaving nothing to verify.

sections.title: Mobile homes, manufactured homes, and mobile home parks
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 550 covers mobile and manufactured homes and the parks that serve them, including how the home connects to its supply, the feeder between the park service and the home, and the disconnecting means at the home. Factory-built homes arrive with their interior wiring already inspected under the federal HUD program, so the site electrician's world is the service, the feeder, and the connection.
• Power supply, 550.10: the home is supplied by a feeder — a permanently installed feeder, or a single listed 50-ampere power-supply cord.
• Disconnecting means, 550.11: one disconnect at or near where the supply enters the home, in a readily accessible location.
• Service equipment, 550.32: on the lot, never in or on the home, within sight and not more than 30 ft from the exterior wall, rated not less than 100 amperes.
• Feeder, 550.33: four insulated conductors with a capacity of not less than 100 amperes.
sections.on_the_job: On a mobile home job, Sharma's scope is normally the park or lot service equipment, the feeder, and the connection — not rewiring the home's interior. Work the four section pages that follow — power supply, disconnecting means, service equipment, and feeder — before pricing any hookup. A typical set: a 100-ampere pedestal within sight and 30 ft of the wall, a four-conductor insulated feeder, and the disconnect where the feeder enters the home.
sections.florida_note: Florida has a large manufactured-home stock, including in Sharma's central Florida counties; confirm with the AHJ whether the home carries a HUD label or a state insignia, because that decides who inspected the interior wiring.

sections.why_it_exists: The split exists because two different inspectors touch the same home. The factory interior is built and inspected under the federal HUD program before the home ever reaches the lot; everything from the park service to the connection point is field work under the NEC and the local AHJ. Knowing where the factory's work ends and yours begins keeps you from owning — or disturbing — wiring another inspector already signed off.
inspection_fails: Service equipment mounted on or in the home, outside the 550.32(B) permanent-foundation exception.

sections.title: Power supply — the home is fed by a feeder
sections.plain_explanation:
A mobile or manufactured home is supplied by a feeder, not by service conductors landed in the home. 550.10(A) allows exactly two forms:
• A single listed 50-ampere mobile home power-supply cord, or
• A permanently installed feeder of fixed wiring.
The cord carries its own rules (550.10(B) through (G)): it is permanently attached to the home's panelboard, it has four conductors with the grounding conductor identified green or green with yellow stripes, it ends in a 3-pole, 4-wire, 50-ampere, 125/250-volt plug cap, and its overall length runs from 21 ft minimum to 36½ ft maximum. It enters the home through the exterior wall, floor, or roof — never through a window or vent.
The permanent feeder also runs four conductors — two ungrounded, an insulated neutral, and a separate equipment grounding conductor — installed by mast or in a raceway (550.10(I)).
Either way, the panelboard inside the home is a feeder panel, never service equipment: the neutral is isolated and the grounds land on their own bus. The one exception is the manufactured home on a permanent foundation that meets 550.32(B): it may be supplied directly by a service, with the service equipment in or on the home.
sections.on_the_job: Manufactured home set in a Marion County park: the lot service equipment sits beside the home, in sight and within 30 ft of the exterior wall, rated not less than 100 A. The home's load fits the cord, so the listed 50-ampere cord does the job — four conductors, 28 ft long, inside the 21 ft to 36½ ft window, plugged into the 50-ampere receptacle in the lot equipment. Inside, land the panelboard as a sub-panel: neutral bar isolated, grounds on a separate bus, no bonding screw. If the home sat on a permanent foundation meeting 550.32(B), the service could land on the home instead — confirm the foundation case before pricing either way.

sections.why_it_exists: The home was wired and inspected at the factory as a load, not as a service. Keeping the supply a feeder means there is exactly one neutral-to-ground bond in the system, at the lot service equipment. A second bond inside the home puts neutral current on the grounding conductor, the chassis, and the metal skirting — invisible until someone touches the home and a wet hose bib at the same time.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the home's main breaker as the service disconnect and bonding the neutral in the home's panel “like a house.” A mobile home is fed by a feeder: the bond lives at the lot service equipment, and the home's panelboard stays a sub-panel with an isolated neutral — on a cord connection and on a permanent feeder alike.

sections.title: Disconnecting means at the home
sections.plain_explanation:
Each mobile or manufactured home has a single disconnecting means — a circuit breaker, or a switch and fuses — at or near the point where the supply cord or the feeder conductors enter the home, in a readily accessible location.
• One disconnect, not two: the whole home shuts off at one obvious place.
• The disconnect may be combined with the branch-circuit protective equipment, so the main breaker in the home's panelboard can serve as the disconnect.
• It pairs with 550.32: one disconnect at the home itself (550.11), and the service equipment disconnect outside, within sight of the home and within 30 ft of its exterior wall (550.32).
sections.on_the_job: On a manufactured-home set or a panel changeout in a Marion County park, walk it in order: pedestal service disconnect outside — within sight and inside 30 ft of the exterior wall — then the home's own single disconnect where the feeder enters. Find it, label it, and test it. If a home shows two mains, or the disconnect is hidden behind stored material, flag it on the ticket — the occupant and the fire department both need one obvious shutoff, and 'the other breaker in the back bedroom' is not it.
sections.why_it_exists: When a manufactured home catches fire or floods, the occupant and the fire department both need one obvious shutoff, findable in the dark, in a hurry. Two mains, or a disconnect buried behind stored furniture, defeat the whole idea — somebody has to know the home is actually off before anyone works or wades in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is merging the two disconnects into one. 550.11 puts a disconnect at the home, where the supply enters; 550.32 puts the service disconnect outside, within sight and within 30 ft of the exterior wall. A job can need both. The reverse trap: insisting the home's disconnect must be a separate switch next to the panel — the panel's main breaker is allowed to be that disconnect.

Home's disconnect blocked by stored material — not readily accessible.

sections.title: Service equipment — in sight and within 30 ft of the home
sections.plain_explanation:
Mobile home service equipment is located adjacent to the home, never mounted in or on it, in sight from the home and not more than 30 ft from its exterior wall. If the service equipment must sit elsewhere on the premises, a disconnecting means suitable for use as service equipment still has to be within sight and within 30 ft of the wall, with grounding at that disconnect per 250.32. The equipment is rated not less than 100 amperes at 120/240 volts and must allow the feeder to be connected by a permanent wiring method. Mounting height is fixed too: the bottom of the enclosure at least 2 ft above the ground, and the disconnect not more than 6 ft 7 in. above the ground or platform. A manufactured home on a permanent foundation that meets the conditions of 550.32(B) is the exception — its service equipment may be installed in or on the home.

Service equipment for a mobile home must be within sight from the home: visible and no more than 50 ft away (see 110.29).

sections.title: The feeder — four insulated conductors, 100-ampere capacity
sections.plain_explanation:
The feeder from the service equipment to the home is four continuous, insulated, color-coded conductors:
• Two ungrounded conductors
• One grounded (neutral) conductor
• One insulated equipment grounding conductor
A bare grounding conductor inside a cable assembly does not count — the ground must be insulated like the rest. Under 550.33(B) the feeder conductors must have a capacity and ampacity of not less than 100 amperes, even when the home's calculated load comes out smaller. Where the conductors are spliced, the splice goes in a suitable junction box — never inside the raceway.
sections.on_the_job: Setting a manufactured home on a lot in Polk County: the park pedestal sits within sight and 30 ft of the wall (550.32), and the feeder trench is open. Pull four insulated conductors every time; standard SER with a bare ground does not make a mobile home feeder. Size for the 100-ampere minimum capacity, and land the insulated ground on the grounding bus at both ends, keeping neutral and ground separate inside the home.

sections.why_it_exists: A mobile home feeder lives underground, where a bare ground corrodes and disappears years before anyone opens the run. The insulated equipment grounding conductor survives the burial, so the fault path back to the service equipment is still there on the day a fault happens. The 100-ampere floor keeps a small calculated load from shrinking the feeder below what the home's service equipment is built for.

sections.title: Recreational vehicles and recreational vehicle parks
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 551 covers recreational vehicles themselves and, more importantly for site work, RV parks — the site supply equipment, receptacle configurations, and grounding for each RV lot. Part VI covers the parks.
• Every site with electrical supply gets site supply equipment with the receptacles travelers carry: 20-ampere, 125-volt; 30-ampere, 125-volt in the TT-30 configuration; and 50-ampere, 125/250-volt.
• The mix is code, not preference: at least 70 percent of sites get a 30-ampere receptacle, at least 40 percent of new sites (20 percent of existing) get a 50-ampere — and every 50-ampere site also carries a 30 (551.71).
• Each site's equipment includes its own disconnect and overcurrent protection, and the receptacles carry the ground-fault protection the article requires.
• Park services and feeders are calculated from the sites: 9,600 VA per 50-ampere site, 3,600 VA per site with 20- and 30-ampere supply, 2,400 VA per 20-ampere-only site, and 600 VA per tent site — then reduced by the demand factors of Table 551.73(A) (551.73).
Park work is a feeder and pedestal job repeated many times, with GFCI and polarity details at every site. It pairs with Article 552, which covers park trailers separately.
sections.on_the_job: A 40-site RV park expansion off US-27: count sites and pedestal types carefully and confirm the supply equipment listing. Do not price park pedestals as ordinary receptacle posts. The code mix drives the count: at least 28 of the 40 sites (70 percent) get 30-ampere receptacles, and at least 16 new sites (40 percent) get 50-ampere supply, each also carrying a 30. Load basis before demand factors: 16 × 9,600 VA + 24 × 3,600 VA = 240,000 VA. Table 551.73(A) then steps that down as sites are added — the difference between a service that prices the job and one that prices Sharma out of it.

sections.why_it_exists: An RV is a dwelling that plugs in outdoors, often on wet ground, plugged and unplugged by the traveling public, not an electrician. The pedestal rules standardize what every traveler finds, put a disconnect and breaker in reach at the site, and put ground-fault protection where hands, water and cord caps meet. The demand table exists because a park never draws full rating at every pedestal at once — sizing without it prices the job out.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calculating an RV park service at the straight sum of the pedestal ratings. Section 551.73 counts each site at its supply rating — 9,600 VA for a 50-ampere site — and then applies the demand factors of Table 551.73(A), which step down as sites are added. Skipping the table oversizes the service badly. The reverse trap is forgetting the mix itself: at least 40 percent of new sites must be 50-ampere sites (551.71).

sections.title: RV site supply equipment — what each pedestal must offer (551.71)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 551.71 is the pedestal page for RV parks. Each RV site with an electrical supply gets site supply equipment — receptacles, a disconnecting means, and overcurrent protection, all at the site. The receptacle mix is set by the section, not by preference:
• Every site: at least one 20-ampere, 125-volt receptacle.
• At least 70 percent of sites: a 30-ampere, 125-volt receptacle in the TT-30 travel-trailer configuration.
• At least 40 percent of new sites — and 20 percent of existing sites: a 50-ampere, 125/250-volt receptacle. Every 50-ampere site also carries a 30-ampere receptacle.
• Ground-fault protection (551.71(F)): the 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles get listed GFCI protection for personnel. The 30- and 50-ampere supply receptacles do not — they are the RV's feeder connection, not general-purpose outlets, and GFCI protection is not required for them.
A pedestal is a small service repeated down a row: rating, configuration, and protection repeat with it.
sections.on_the_job: New 50-site park outside Ocala: the mix is code math before it is a purchase order. All 50 sites get the 20-ampere receptacle. At least 35 sites — 70 percent — get the TT-30. At least 20 sites — 40 percent of new — get the 50-ampere, 125/250-volt receptacle, and each of those 20 also carries a 30. The owner wants 50-ampere supply at every site for the winter season; that is permitted, and it feeds the 551.73 load math at 9,600 VA a site. On the existing park across the road, added 50-ampere sites only have to reach the 20 percent floor for existing sites. Confirm who furnishes the pedestals before the number is final.

sections.why_it_exists: A traveler plugs a 40 ft RV into a pedestal in the rain, at night, with wet hands and a cord dragged through wet grass. The GFCI protects the person at the small receptacle used for outdoor equipment, the disconnect and breaker at the site keep a fault local to one site, and the standard configurations mean the plug in the traveler's hand fits a pedestal at any park in the country.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “every pedestal receptacle needs GFCI, including the 50-ampere.” 551.71(F) limits GFCI protection to the 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles. The 30- and 50-ampere receptacles are the RV's feeder connection — the Code deliberately leaves them off the GFCI list, because RV appliance leakage can exceed what a personnel GFCI allows.

sections.title: Sizing RV park services and feeders (551.73)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 551.73 calculates an RV park's service and feeders from the sites themselves.
• The load basis (551.73(A)): 9,600 volt-amperes per site with 50-ampere, 208Y/120V or 120/240V supply; 3,600 volt-amperes per site with both 20- and 30-ampere supply; 2,400 volt-amperes per site with only 20-ampere supply; and 600 volt-amperes per site with only 20-ampere supply dedicated to tent sites. A site with several receptacles counts once, at its highest-rated supply.
• The total is then reduced by the demand factors of Table 551.73(A), which step down as the number of sites grows — 100 percent for one site, 50 percent at 10 to 12 sites, and 41 percent at 36 sites and above — because a whole park never draws full load at every pedestal at once.
• The demand factors apply to the sites only. Bathhouses, recreation buildings, pools, and similar park loads are calculated separately and added at full value.
The demand table is not optional color: on a forty-site park it is the difference between a service that prices the job and one that prices Sharma out of it.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: ten sites, all 50-ampere — 10 × 9,600 = 96,000 VA connected. Table 551.73(A) gives 50 percent for 10 to 12 sites, so the demand load is 48,000 VA — at 240 volts, a 200-ampere service. Price the same park without the table and you are quoting a 400-ampere service nobody needs. Scale it up: forty 50-ampere sites are 384,000 VA connected; the 41 percent factor gives 157,440 VA, about 656 amperes at 240 volts — before the bathhouse and laundry are added separately, at full load. Pull the factor for the actual site count from the printed table on the worksheet; do not carry a remembered percentage between jobs.

sections.why_it_exists: Pedestals are sized for the biggest rig that might plug in, but a park's rigs cycle air conditioners, water heaters, and chargers at different times. Sizing the service on the straight sum buys copper for a peak that never happens. The demand table is the Code's measured diversity for parks: enough headroom for a full winter weekend, without a service sized for a fantasy.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is skipping the table in either direction. Sizing at 100 percent “to be safe” prices Sharma out of the job — and applying the 41 percent floor to a 10-site park undersizes it, because 10 to 12 sites take 50 percent. The factor follows the site count on the printed table, every time.

sections.title: Park trailers
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 552 covers park trailers — the trailer-type units built for park placement rather than highway travel, defined around a size threshold that separates them from recreational vehicles. Its rules parallel the mobile home and RV articles for supply and connection. Confusing a park trailer with an RV or a mobile home sends the job to the wrong article, so identification comes first.

Identification turns on the definition: a park trailer is built on a single chassis on wheels and, in its set-up mode, stays at or under 400 square feet of gross area — bigger or permanently sited units fall to other articles. Supply follows the unit's listing: park trailers are typically served by a cord connection or a permanent feeder sized to the unit's load under this article, with the disconnect and protection at the site. When the paperwork and the unit disagree, the nameplate and listing govern.
sections.on_the_job: Read the unit's label and paperwork before choosing between 550, 551, and 552. When the unit type is unclear, ask the AHJ rather than guessing the article.

sections.title: Article 553 — deleted in 2020 (floating buildings now live in Article 555, Part III)
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 553 no longer exists as its own article.
• In the 2020 NEC it was deleted, and its subject — floating buildings, structures supported by water rather than by a foundation, other than boats — was folded into Article 555 as its Part III (555.50 and following).
• The substance carried over: the shore-to-building supply, service equipment and disconnecting means located on land rather than on the floating structure, and ground-fault protection for the supply.
• A floating building is a structure, not a vessel — it is worked like a building that happens to float.
Work a floating building from Article 555, Part III — not from an old 553 printout.
sections.on_the_job: Floating restaurant on a lakefront lot in Tavares. The service equipment and the disconnect go on adjacent land, not on the floating structure, and the feeder crosses from the shore disconnect to the building. Coordinate early with the marina scope in Article 555 so the two articles do not get priced twice or missed entirely — the shore work, the disconnect and the ground-fault protection each belong in one takeoff line, not both.
sections.florida_note: Coastal and lakefront AHJs in Florida look hard at floating structures; confirm the local position on shore disconnect placement before the takeoff is final.
sections.why_it_exists: A floating building moves with the water, so anything mounted on it flexes, chafes and corrodes faster than the same gear on land. Keeping the service equipment and the disconnect on solid ground gives firefighters and maintenance crews a disconnect they can reach without boarding a moving structure. Ground-fault protection on the supply matters because a fault on a floating structure leaks straight into the water where people swim.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is working from an old Article 553 printout or a pre-2020 code book. 553 was deleted in 2020, so an answer — or a takeoff — built on 553 misses that the rules now sit in Article 555, Part III, alongside the marina rules the same crew is already working from.

sections.title: Marinas, boatyards, floating buildings, and docking facilities
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 555 covers wiring and equipment at fixed and floating piers, marinas, boatyards, boathouses, and residential and commercial docking facilities, plus floating buildings in their own part of the article. 555.1 expressly includes docking facilities associated with one-family dwellings, so a private residential dock is inside this article — not an AHJ judgment call.
• The driving hazard is electric shock drowning: stray current in the water around an energized boat or dock can paralyze a swimmer without any visible warning.
• The electrical datum plane (555.3) sets the heights: on a floating pier, 30 in above the water level and at least 12 in above the deck; on land, 2 ft above the highest tide or water level.
• Receptacles sit at least 12 in above the deck and never below the datum plane (555.33); shore power receptacles are rated not less than 30 A.
• Ground-fault protection comes in layers (555.35): shore power receptacles get equipment protection set at not more than 30 mA, feeders and branch circuits to a dock or slip get equipment protection at not more than 100 mA, and ordinary 15- and 20-ampere receptacles get Class A GFCI protection for people.
• The service equipment stays on land, adjacent to the structure it serves — never on or in the floating structure (555.4).
sections.on_the_job: A homeowner on a Lake County canal calls: the pedestal trips every time the boat lift runs. Treat every marina circuit as life-safety work. Test the ground-fault devices, verify the bonding, and never defeat a tripping device to keep a boat powered. The shore power receptacle's equipment protection is set at not more than 30 mA and the feeder protection at not more than 100 mA, so find which layer is tripping and fix the fault it found. If a pedestal keeps tripping, the trip is the protection working.

sections.florida_note: Florida is Sharma's marina state — salt water corrosion, storm surge, and coastal AHJs all bear on this work; use marine-listed equipment and confirm the local datum and inspection practice before bidding coastal docks.

sections.title: Electrical datum plane — heights above the water
sections.plain_explanation:
The electrical datum plane is the reference height above the water below which certain equipment, connections, and receptacles may not be installed. 555.3 sets the plane by the kind of structure:
• Floating piers and floating facilities, 555.3(A): the plane is 30 in above the water level, and at least 12 in above the deck level.
• Land areas subject to tidal fluctuation, 555.3(B): the plane is 2 ft above the highest tide level for the area, under normal circumstances.
• Land areas not subject to tidal fluctuation, 555.3(C): the plane is 2 ft above the highest water level for the area, under normal circumstances.
Normal circumstances is the key phrase. The plane is figured from ordinary high water — not from the water level on the day of the install, and not from storm surge.
sections.on_the_job: Establish the datum line on site with the marina operator and mark it on the pier before rough-in — then set nothing the article restricts below it. Re-check after any deck or float work that changes deck height. On a floating dock on a Central Florida lake, work both numbers — 30 in above the water and at least 12 in above the deck — and hold the higher line. The same line controls the shore power receptacles: 555.33 keeps them at least 12 in above the deck and never below the datum plane.

sections.why_it_exists: Water rises. Equipment set by eye on a calm day sits under water at the next ordinary high tide, and energized equipment in the water is a shock hazard for everyone in it. The datum plane turns 'high enough' into a number the whole job can measure against.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is using the floating-pier numbers everywhere. Thirty inches above the water is the floating case, 555.3(A). A fixed installation on tidal land uses 2 ft above the highest tide level, and the measurement starts from the highest normal level — not from the water you see at low tide on rough-in day.

sections.title: Location of service equipment — on land, not on the structure
sections.plain_explanation:
The service equipment for a floating building, dock, or marina is installed on land, adjacent to the structure it serves — never on or in the floating structure itself. A floating structure rides up and down with the water, so the service stays on solid ground, where it can be reached and worked on like any other service. Everything downstream of it — the feeders out along the pier — is supplied from that shore-side point.
• The service equipment sits on land, adjacent to the structure it serves
• It is never installed on or in a floating building or a floating dock
• Feeders run from that shore-side service out along the pier to the shore-power pedestals and dock loads
• Heights near the water still have to respect the electrical datum plane in 555.3 — for floating piers, 30 in above the water level and at least 12 in above the deck level
sections.on_the_job: Set the service on land next to the dock or marina it serves and run the feeder out to the pier from there. If a plan or an existing installation shows the service mounted on a floating dock, flag it before rough-in — that location fails this section. At a Lake County marina re-power, the pattern is the meter and main disconnect on land by the seawall, with feeders in conduit along the fixed pier to the floating slips. If the existing service is found on the floating dock, price the relocation to land in the bid — leaving it there is not something an inspector can pass.

sections.why_it_exists: A floating dock is a moving platform. It rises and falls with tide and wake, flexes every conductor attached to it, and can swamp, break loose or sink in a storm. Service equipment belongs where it stays put: on land, where the utility connection is stable, the disconnect is reachable in an emergency, and nobody has to work on live service equipment while standing on a wet, moving platform.

sections.title: Pier power distribution — the 250-volt limit
sections.plain_explanation:
Pier power distribution systems are limited to 250 volts phase to phase.
• The cap is on the distribution system serving the pier — the feeders and branch circuits that run the docking facility.
• The single exception is an engineered installation: where qualified personnel service the equipment under engineering supervision, the system may run above 250 volts, but never above 600 volts phase to phase.
• Ordinary marina and dock work is designed well under the cap, at the standard voltages — the higher band is not a field upgrade.
• The cap is measured phase to phase, so a three-phase pier system is judged on its phase-to-phase voltage, not phase to ground.
sections.on_the_job: Read the distribution voltage on the plans before ordering gear. If a pier design shows more than 250 volts phase to phase, stop and confirm the qualified-personnel and engineering-supervision conditions are actually part of the job — that call belongs to the engineer, not the crew. A residential dock or a small marina panel at the standard single-phase voltages never comes near the cap; the flag goes up when a plan set shows a three-phase feeder above 250 volts headed down the pier.
sections.why_it_exists: A pier is a wet, public place. Boaters, kids, and dock hands — not electricians — plug in, unplug, and handle equipment standing in or beside the water. Capping the distribution voltage keeps the shock and fault energy on the pier at the level ordinary marine equipment and ordinary users are built around.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reading the exception as a permission slip. 'Our shop has qualified electricians' is not enough — the exception needs qualified personnel servicing the equipment under engineering supervision as part of the installation, and 600 volts is the absolute ceiling, not a design target. For ordinary pier work the answer stays 250 volts phase to phase.

sections.title: Boat hoists — GFCI protection at dwelling docks
sections.plain_explanation: A boat hoist rated not more than 240 volts at a dwelling unit docking facility must have GFCI protection. The 2020 edition moved this rule out of 210.8(C) and into Article 555, with the rest of the marina and dock rules. It is the lift on a house dock that raises the boat out of the water — a motor, a control pendant, and people standing on a wet dock, often barefoot, which is exactly the combination the GFCI is there for. The rule covers the hoist itself; shore-power receptacles and the rest of the dock carry their own Article 555 rules on their own pages.
sections.on_the_job: On a residential dock job on the Winter Park chain of lakes or a Lake County lakefront, feed the hoist from the dock panel through GFCI protection and test it at trim with the hoist under load. If an existing hoist outlet has no GFCI protection, call it out to the owner in writing — a hoist motor fault over water is the shock path this rule exists to break, and 'it worked when we got here' is not a defense anybody wants to make later.
sections.why_it_exists: Water changes the shock math. A hoist motor fault can energize the hoist frame, the dock hardware, and the water around the ladder at the same time, and a person climbing out of the water is a near-perfect ground path. The GFCI watches for current leaking out of the circuit and trips in a fraction of a cycle — before the fault current through a swimmer becomes fatal.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering 210.8(C). That was the rule's home before 2020; the 2020 edition moved boat hoists into 555.9, with the other dock rules. The second trap is scope: 555.9 covers hoists at dwelling docking facilities — a commercial marina hoist is a different conversation, and a hoist rated over 240 volts is outside this section entirely.

sections.title: Warning signs — the shock hazard notice
sections.plain_explanation:
A permanent safety sign is required at docking facilities, boatyards and marinas, warning of the electrical shock hazard in the water.
• The sign must warn with effective words, colors or symbols meeting 110.21(B)(1).
• It must be durable enough to withstand the environment.
• It must be clearly visible from all approaches to the facility.
• At a minimum it must state: WARNING — POTENTIAL SHOCK HAZARD — ELECTRICAL CURRENTS MAY BE PRESENT IN THE WATER.
• A sign that can only be seen from inside the facility does not comply — visibility is judged from the approaches.
This is the electric shock drowning warning, and the sign is part of the installation, not an extra.
sections.on_the_job: Final walk at a small marina in Sanford. Put the sign in the job scope and photograph it at final — the job can fail inspection for a missing sign even when every circuit is right. Mount it at the dock entrance, facing the approach, where someone heading for the water will actually see it, not on the back of the service equipment where only the electrician ever looks.
sections.figure_idea: Sign detail: warning header over the required wording in three lines, shown mounted at a dock entrance.
sections.why_it_exists: Electric shock drowning kills quietly: a swimmer near a leaking boat or a faulted dock is paralyzed by current in the water and slips under without a mark on them. Nobody can see electricity in water, so the warning has to do the seeing. A sign at every approach is the last chance to keep swimmers out of water that a fault could energize at any moment.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the sign as the owner's problem or a closeout extra. 555.10 makes it part of the installation, with required wording. A paraphrased warning — 'Danger: electricity in water' — is wrong; the minimum wording is set by the section, and the sign has to be visible from all approaches, not just from the office door.

Sign wording paraphrased instead of the required minimum text.
Sign mounted where approaching visitors cannot see it — back of the service equipment.

sections.title: Bonding at marinas and docking facilities
sections.plain_explanation:
555.13 is the bonding rule for marinas, boatyards, and docking facilities — including the private dock at a one-family dwelling.
• What gets bonded: metal parts in contact with the water, metal piping, and non-current-carrying metal parts that are likely to become energized — ladders, lifts, hoists, and metal framing all read as one list.
• Where it lands: every one of those parts bonds back to the grounding bus in the panelboard that serves the dock. Not to a rod driven at the pier, and not to the nearest green screw — to the panelboard grounding bus.
• The conductor: solid copper, insulated, covered, or bare, and not smaller than 8 AWG.
• The point is equipotential: dock metal, boat metal, and the water around them are held at the same voltage, so a fault raises everything together and the ground-fault protection trips, instead of leaving one ladder hot against the water.
• Bonding is one layer of the marina system. Shore power receptacles get ground-fault protection of equipment at not more than 30 milliamperes, and feeders to the dock at not more than 100 milliamperes (555.35), and equipment heights are set off the electrical datum plane (555.3).
sections.on_the_job: Residential dock on a Marion County lake: the takeoff bonds the aluminum ladder, the boat lift frame, and the metal water piping back to the panelboard grounding bus with a continuous run of 8 AWG solid copper, protected where the run crosses the pier framing. At trim, the crew tests continuity from the farthest lift bolt back to the bus — a bonding jumper cut by later dock work is a silent failure, and continuity is the last thing checked before the job is called done.

nec2023_change.change: Metal parts already grounded through a branch-circuit or feeder equipment grounding conductor no longer need their own 8 AWG bonding conductor. Everything else still bonds to the panelboard grounding bus. Metal parts already connected to a branch-circuit or feeder equipment grounding conductor (EGC) no longer need a separate bonding conductor.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 555.13 Marina bonding

sections.why_it_exists: The killer at a dock is electric shock drowning. A fault on a boat or lift puts current into the water, and the voltage gradient around the hull can paralyze a swimmer who never touches anything metal. Bonding every metal part back to the panelboard bus holds the dock, the boat, and the water at one potential and gives fault current a solid path back to trip the protection. An unbonded ladder next to an energized hull is the accident this section exists to prevent.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is driving a ground rod at the end of the pier and calling the dock 'bonded.' A rod connects the metal to the earth; 555.13 bonds it to the grounding bus in the panelboard, which is what makes the dock one equipotential system and gives a fault a path that trips the breaker. Second trap: grabbing stranded 8 AWG because it is on the truck. The 2020 text calls for solid copper.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for shore power connections (2020 section 555.36)
sections.plain_explanation:
Each boat's shore power connection needs its own disconnecting means that isolates that boat from its supply.
• The disconnect is a circuit breaker, a switch, or both.
• It is identified to show which receptacle it controls.
• It is readily accessible, and it sits ahead of the receptacle in the circuit.
• It is located not more than 30 in from the receptacle it controls.
Breakers or switches inside a marine power outlet can serve as this disconnect when they meet those conditions.
The disconnect belongs to the connection, not to the dock — that is the whole shape of the rule.
sections.on_the_job: Label every pedestal disconnect with the slip and receptacle it controls, and measure the 30-inch limit before the pedestal is set. A boater in the dark needs to kill one connection, not the whole dock. On a two-pedestal replacement, that means each pedestal carries its own breaker for its own receptacle — a shared disconnect at the head of the dock does not satisfy this section, even if it is labeled.
sections.sharma_note: This is the 2020 section number, 555.36. The older number 555.17 is not the 2020 section, and 555.36 is not a 2023-only number.

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: each marina power outlet or enclosure feeding shore power needs a listed emergency shutoff marked for that use, within sight of it. A breaker handle doesn't count. Each marina power outlet or enclosure that feeds boats needs its own listed emergency shutoff within sight, marked with the words "Emergency Shutoff" (555.36(C)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 555.36 Shore power emergency shutoff

sections.why_it_exists: When a boat has an electrical fire, a failed shore cord, or a fault near someone in the water, the power to that one boat has to die fast — by whoever is standing there, in the dark, without hunting through a dock full of pedestals. One identified disconnect within reach of the receptacle makes that a single motion.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is one main disconnect at the head of the dock for every boat. 555.36 wants a disconnect per connection, identified, within 30 in of its receptacle. The second trap runs the other way: breakers inside the marine power outlet are allowed to serve as the disconnect when they meet the conditions — 'the breaker doesn't count' is the 2023 emergency-shutoff rule, not the 2020 disconnect rule.

sections.title: Receptacles at marinas and docking facilities (2020 section 555.33)
sections.plain_explanation:
555.33 is where the 2020 NEC keeps the receptacle rules for marinas and docking facilities.
• Every receptacle mounts at least 12 in above the deck surface, and never below the electrical datum plane.
• Shore power receptacles are part of a listed marine power outlet, installed in a listed enclosure protected from the weather, and rated not less than 30 A.
• Shore power receptacles rated 60 A or more are the pin-and-sleeve type.
• Receptacles other than shore power get GFCI protection under 210.8.
• A replacement receptacle has to meet this section too.
Height, listing and location work together — a correct receptacle set too low still fails.
sections.on_the_job: Pedestal replacement at a marina in Cape Canaveral, one dock with 18 slips. Set receptacle heights from the finished deck — 12 in minimum — and re-check them if the decking is replaced after rough-in, because new deck boards over old stringers can eat the clearance. Use only marine power outlets listed for shore power service where boats connect; a standard weatherproof receptacle in a bell box is not a shore power outlet and will not pass.
sections.sharma_note: This is the 2020 section number, 555.33. The older number 555.19 is not the 2020 section, and 555.33 is not a 2023-only number.
sections.why_it_exists: A marina deck is wet, salty and walked on barefoot, and the water level moves. A receptacle down at deck level sits in wash water and splash, corrodes fast, and puts line voltage within reach of wet hands and wet feet. The datum plane rule ties the mounting height to the water level the AHJ designs for, not just to the boards under your boots today.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the old section number: answers keyed to 555.19 come from a pre-2020 book. In 2020 the receptacle rules are at 555.33. The second trap is height alone — a receptacle 12 in above the deck that still sits below the electrical datum plane fails.

sections.title: Ground-fault protection — GFPE and GFCI at marinas
sections.plain_explanation:
The 2020 edition organizes this section into three clear layers of ground-fault protection.
• Shore power receptacles get individual ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) set to open at not more than 30 mA.
• 15- and 20-ampere receptacles other than shore power get Class A GFCI protection for people.
• Feeder and branch circuit conductors supplying a dock or slip get GFPE set at not more than 100 mA.
GFPE protects equipment and wiring at milliampere levels far above the 4 to 6 mA Class A GFCI trip that protects people, so the two are not interchangeable labels.
sections.on_the_job: Pedestal replacement at a boatyard in Fort Pierce, 24 slips on two feeders. Build the protection in layers exactly as the design shows — 30 mA GFPE at each shore power receptacle, Class A GFCI on the 15 and 20 A convenience receptacles, 100 mA GFPE on the feeders — and record the trip settings at startup. Never swap a GFPE device for an ordinary breaker because a boat keeps tripping it; find the leaking boat instead.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 caution: Sharma's residential DFN breaker is a personnel GFCI and AFCI device. It is not, by itself, the GFPE protection this section requires at 30 and 100 milliamperes — do not carry the house device pattern onto a dock without Mike Holt confirming the specified marina equipment.
sections.figure_idea: Layer diagram: shore receptacle with 30 milliampere GFPE, general receptacle with Class A GFCI, feeder with 100 milliampere GFPE, stacked as three bands.
sections.florida_note: Florida coastal AHJs test marina ground-fault protection seriously after electric shock drowning incidents nationally; expect the settings and signage to be checked at final.

nec2023_change.change: GFCI now reaches non-shore-power dock outlets on circuits no higher than 150 volts to ground and 60 amps (100 amps three-phase), plus boat hoists at every dock. Leakage testers must be listed from 2026. Non-shore-power outlets, lights and equipment included, need GFCI when the circuit is no higher than 150 volts to ground and 60 amps (100 amps three-phase).

sections.why_it_exists: Stray current in marina water paralyzes a swimmer without ever tripping an ordinary breaker — that is electric shock drowning. Leakage from one boat or one damaged cord can energize the water around a whole dock. Layered protection catches leakage at the receptacle and again at the feeder, at levels high enough that normal boat leakage does not black out the dock, and low enough to clear a real fault.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating GFPE and GFCI as one device with two names. A Class A GFCI trips at 4 to 6 mA to protect people. The shore power GFPE is set at 30 mA and the feeder GFPE at 100 mA, both protecting equipment and wiring. An answer that puts a personnel GFCI where the section wants 100 mA feeder GFPE — or the reverse — is wrong both ways.

sections.title: Temporary installations — jobsite power
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 590 covers power and lighting installed for a limited time:
• Construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair and demolition work.
• Holiday and decorative installations, and similar short-term uses.
• Emergencies, experiments and testing.
Chapters 1 through 4 still apply except where this article specifically changes them. The article relaxes a few wiring methods for the temporary case, but the safety core stays fully in force: overcurrent protection, grounding, and GFCI protection for people. Time is part of the rule — under 590.3, construction power lasts for the duration of the work, and holiday and decorative installations are limited to 90 days.
• Every 125-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30-ampere receptacle outlet that is not part of the permanent wiring needs GFCI protection for personnel (590.6(A)(1)).
• On a construction site, receptacles may not share a branch circuit with temporary lighting, and cords and cables used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on the floor or ground (590.4).
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's standard temp pole on a Marion Oaks rough-in: meter and a Siemens load center on the pole, two 20-ampere GFCI-protected receptacles for the crew's tools, and a ground rod driven its full 8 ft with the GEC clamped above grade where it can be inspected. The temp service paperwork carries a removal date; when the permanent service is energized and accepted, the pole comes out instead of lingering for the next trade to trip over.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 does not set temp panel sizes, but Sharma temp work still uses listed gear and Siemens breakers in our own panels per S-02. Temp is not a license for mixed-brand breaker swapping (S-03).
sections.figure_idea: Temp pole sketch: meter, panel, GFCI receptacles, support and grounding, labeled as a field checklist figure.
sections.why_it_exists: Temporary power is the most abused wiring on any site: cords run over by lifts, panels rained on, spider boxes moved daily by every trade. The hazard is not lower because the installation is temporary — the exposure is higher. That is why the article trades method flexibility for an unrelaxed core of GFCI protection, grounding and overcurrent protection.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “GFCI is not required — it is only temporary power.” 590.6(A)(1) requires GFCI protection for personnel on the 125-volt 15-, 20- and 30-ampere receptacle outlets used for the work, temporary or not. The second trap: holiday lighting on a 90-day limit treated as a permanent installation.

sections.title: Time constraints on temporary installations
sections.plain_explanation:
590.3 is the clock on every temporary installation. Temporary wiring is permitted only for the period the work actually lasts — and each kind of use gets its own limit:
• During the period of construction (590.3(A)): construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair, and demolition power stays for that work. There is no day count — the limit is the job itself.
• 90 days (590.3(B)): holiday decorative lighting and similar decorative uses get a hard cap of 90 days, and then the temporary power comes out.
• Emergencies and tests (590.3(C)): emergencies, tests, experiments, and developmental work may use temporary wiring for the duration the need actually lasts.
• Removal (590.3(D)): whatever the use, temporary wiring must be removed immediately upon completion of the purpose it was installed for. Temporary wiring that quietly becomes permanent is a violation, not a value add.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's standard temp pole on a Marion Oaks rough-in goes in with a removal date written on the temp service paperwork. The permanent service is energized and accepted, and the pole comes out that same week instead of lingering for the next trade to trip over. The mirror case is retail holiday lighting: a storefront display wired in early November hits its 90 days at the end of January, and the calendar — not the tenant's memory — says when it is removed.
sections.why_it_exists: Article 590 trades method flexibility for time. Cords, temp panels, and relaxed methods survive a supervised construction site because everyone knows they are coming out. Left in place, they take permanent-service abuse with temporary-grade protection — cords get driven over, panels weather, and nobody owns the removal. The time limits are what keep the trade fair: the installation is only as safe as the promise that it ends.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is applying the 90-day cap to construction power. The 90 days in 590.3(B) belongs to holiday decorative lighting and similar uses only. sections.title: General requirements for temporary wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
This is the working section of the article. A temporary service is installed to the service rules of Article 230, feeders and branch circuits keep the overcurrent protection of Article 240 (590.4(B) and (C)), and hard or extra-hard usage cords and cables do much of the distribution work.
• Receptacles on a branch circuit may not share it with temporary lighting on a construction site (590.4(D)).
• Receptacles in wet locations need weatherproof protection with a plug inserted — an in-use cover, not a flip lid.
• Every temporary circuit needs a way to disconnect all its ungrounded conductors.
• Lamps for general illumination need protection from accidental contact or breakage — a suitable fixture or lampholder with a guard (590.4(F)).
• Splices need a box, conduit body, or other enclosure with a cover (590.4(G)). The construction-site exceptions cover splices in cord and cable assemblies and in permanent wiring used temporarily — not open-air twisted joints.
• Cables and cords used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on the ground or floor — support them, protect them where they cross doorways and pinch points, or use the extension cord and protection routes the section actually allows.
sections.on_the_job: Walk a temp installation weekly: guards on lamps, covers on splice boxes, cords up off the ground and out of doorways, and disconnects working. Most temp-power citations are housekeeping items from this one section. On a multi-story build-out, give the weekly walk a route: spider boxes fed with cords supported overhead instead of lying in the walk path, string lights with every guard in place, in-use covers on the receptacles at the wet deck, and the temp panel disconnects exercised so they still open every ungrounded conductor.

nec2023_change.change: Eliminated some existing text concerning various socket styles at Section 590.4(F), and the words "metal guarded sockets" and "metal guard" were added.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 590.4(F) Lamp Protection

sections.why_it_exists: Temporary wiring gets dragged, driven over, rained on, and reworked daily by every trade on the site. The guards, covers, enclosures, and support rules in this section are what stand between that abuse and a broken lamp, an open splice, or a cord cut in a doorway — the three ways temp power starts fires and shocks workers.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the word "temporary" itself: it does not relax the rest of the Code. Article 590 modifies specific rules — services still follow Article 230 and overcurrent protection still follows Article 240. The second trap is the shared circuit: on a construction site, receptacles may not share a branch circuit with temporary lighting, even though the same layout would be legal in finished work.
