sections.title: GFCI protection and the assured grounding program
sections.plain_explanation:
Receptacles that supply temporary power for construction style work need GFCI protection for personnel: the 125-volt, 15-, 20-, and 30-ampere receptacles are covered directly by 590.6(A)(1) and (A)(2); 125/250-volt receptacles join the GFCI list only under (A)(3), and only where they are receptacle outlets on a portable generator rated not greater than 15 kW, including receptacles that are part of the building's permanent wiring when they are being used for the temporary work. For receptacles outside that list, the choice is GFCI protection or a written assured equipment grounding conductor program with documented testing of cords and equipment. All receptacles used for temporary power are of the grounding type.

Where the assured equipment grounding conductor program covers the receptacles outside the GFCI list, the NEC (590.6(B)(2)) requires written procedures and tests before first use on site, when there is evidence of damage, before equipment is returned to service after repairs, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months, recorded and made available to the AHJ. OSHA 29 CFR 1926.404(b)(1)(iii), not the NEC, adds the following details: before first use, before equipment is returned to service after a repair, after any incident that could reasonably be suspected of having caused damage, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months — 6 months only for cord sets and receptacles that are fixed in place and not exposed to damage. Each test verifies the equipment grounding conductor's continuity and that it terminates correctly, and the program is documented, by color coding or tagging and by records. An undocumented program is treated as no program. In NEC 2020 the GFCI scope is: (A)(1) all 125V, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30A receptacle outlets that are not part of the permanent wiring and are in use by personnel; (A)(2) receptacles of any other rating, including the building's permanent receptacles, used to supply temporary power to equipment used by personnel during construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair or demolition — GFCI protection or a listed cord set or device with listed GFCI protection; (A)(3) 125V and 125/250V, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30A receptacle outlets on a portable generator rated 15 kW or less — listed GFCI protection. The 6-month interval for fixed cord sets and receptacles and the color coding are OSHA rules, not NEC rules.
sections.on_the_job: Test temp GFCI devices on a schedule and keep the test log with the temp panel. If a site runs an assured grounding program instead for the larger receptacles, the paperwork and cord color coding have to exist before the inspector asks, not after.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 caution: a DFN breaker feeding a receptacle can be the GFCI method on a house's permanent wiring used temporarily, but a spider box or temp panel on site needs its own GFCI protection verified device by device — do not assume the upstream house pattern covers a jobsite distribution box.

sections.title: Overcurrent devices in temporary installations — new in 2020
sections.plain_explanation:
This section was added in the 2020 edition, and it speaks to the reused breakers and fuses that end up in temp panels.
• Where reused (590.8(A)): an overcurrent device that has been used before may go into a temporary installation only after it is examined, to confirm it has been properly installed, has been properly maintained, and shows no evidence of impending failure — arcing, overheating, loose or bound parts, visible damage, or deterioration.
• Current-limiting service devices (590.8(B)): the overcurrent devices for a temporary service fed from a solidly grounded wye system of more than 150 volts to ground, but not over 1000 volts phase-to-phase, must be of the current-limiting type. A 277/480 volt temp service is the common case. The 2020 text sets no fault-current threshold for this rule.
• The section closes the old habit of treating the temp panel as a junk drawer for retired breakers: a device with an unknown history does not get a second life protecting temporary wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Retire damaged or unknown-history breakers instead of cycling them into temp panels. When a temp service is large, confirm the current-limiting requirement with Mike Holt at takeoff, not at energization. On a 277/480 volt temp service for a commercial build-out, spec current-limiting breakers or fuses in the temp panel from the start: that service is over 150 volts to ground, so 590.8(B) applies before the first circuit is pulled. On the 120/208 volt spider boxes, the foreman examines every reused breaker at setup — heat discoloration, a loose handle, or a cracked case sends it to the dumpster, not back into the box.
sections.sharma_note: S-03 reinforces this: breakers go only in panels they are listed for, temp panels included.

nec2023_change.change: Temporary services on 3-phase wye systems over 150 volts to ground now need current-limiting overcurrent devices only when available fault current exceeds 10,000 amps. Current-limiting service overcurrent devices are now needed only when the available fault current goes above 10,000 amps.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 590.8 Temporary service overcurrent devices

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker that has already cleared faults, sat in a damp gang box, or been swapped from panel to panel may not open when it should. Temporary wiring is handled, moved, and reworked more than any other wiring on the job, so it leans hardest on its overcurrent devices. The current-limiting rule for the bigger wye services also keeps fault energy down where a temp service ties into a stiff utility source.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is importing the 2023 threshold into a 2020 answer. Under the 2020 text, a 277/480 volt temporary service needs current-limiting overcurrent devices because it is a solidly grounded wye system over 150 volts to ground — the 2020 rule has no 10,000-ampere trigger. "Only when the available fault current exceeds 10,000 amps" is the 2023 revision; it is wrong on a 2020 exam and wrong on a 2020 permit.
